People explain a life, or the world, by fitting it to one of a small number of
stories. The sources below each describe that from a different side.

## Sources

- **The Seven Basic Plots.** Christopher Booker's book, which sorts stories
  into seven plots: overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, voyage
  and return, comedy, tragedy and rebirth.
- **The hero's journey.** Joseph Campbell's pattern from *The Hero with a
  Thousand Faces*: a hero leaves the ordinary world, is tested, and comes home
  changed.
- **The Power of Myth.** Bill Moyers's interviews with Joseph Campbell,
  broadcast on PBS in 1988.
- **[Be suspicious of simple stories](https://www.ted.com/talks/tyler_cowen_be_suspicious_of_stories).**
  Tyler Cowen at TEDxMidAtlantic, November 2009, on the power of stories and
  their danger. A story is a filter that keeps some information and leaves the
  rest out, and Cowen is most suspicious of the stories he finds most
  inspiring. He cites Booker's seven plots.

## Freud and Jung

Both [Freud](../people/freud.qmd) and [Jung](../people/jung.qmd) are about
constructing narratives and telling stories. The observation came while
listening to Andrew Scull, a historian of psychiatry, on the
[Lex Fridman Podcast, episode 502](https://open.spotify.com/episode/082a1V6nazH9ZZqskV1vfz).

## Related Notes

- [The Black Swan](../books/black-swan.qmd). Taleb on narrative: people look
  for a story where none exists.
